newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 7.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- COSTAIN PUTS NEW CHAIRMAN INTO FRONT LINE

Troubled contractor Costain yesterday held its fourth shareholder meeting in 12 months. The meeting was disrupted by protesters, targeting the company because of its Newbury bypass contract. Malaysian Dr Azman Firdaus was elected chairman.
-- PENSIONS AT WICKES ANGER INVESTORS

Do-it-yourself retailer Wickes was yesterday attacked by shareholders for paying pensions to its non-executive directors. The attack came at a meeting held to approve a 53 million pound stg rescue rights issue, which was passed overwhelmingly. The company is struggling to recover from a serious fraud in its buying department seven months ago.
-- ELEVENTH-HOUR DRAMA IN BATTLE FOR FOREST

The battle for control of Nottingham Forest intensified yesterday when Grant Bovey of Watershed Pictures re-entered the fight. Meanwhile, Lawrie Lewis of Monte Carlo switched sides from the consortium led by former Tottenham Hotspur chairman Irving Scholar to that headed by rail entrepreneur Sandy Anderson. Nigel Wray of Burford property group entered the fight in the weekend, backing a new 17.75 million pound stg bid from Mr Scholar. The Anderson consortium was last night considering adding a cash offer to its bid. Forest shareholders were due to vote on the Anderson bid last night.
THE TIMES
-- WOOLWICH SHARE BONANZA OFFERS AVERAGE OF 1,200 POUNDS

If the members of the Woolwich Building Society approve the society's conversion to a bank, they will receive shares worth 1,200 pounds stg on average, up to a maximum of 5,437 pounds stg. The transfer document published by the Woolwich yesterday values the society at between 2.96 and 3.38 billion pounds stg.

The society also said yesterday that had it known about proposed changes to conversion rules contained in the new Building Societies Bill in advance, it would have pressed ahead with mergers and acquisitions before it came to the stock market.
-- GB RAILWAYS MAKES EXPRESS START ON AIM GB

Railways more than doubled its market value yesterday after one day of trading on the Alternative Investment Market. The company winner of the Anglia rail franchise started running the London to Norwich train service on Sunday. The shares, placed with institutions at 100p, closed at 210.5p, leaving the company valued at 18.4 million pounds stg.
-- WARBURG LOSES 1 MILLION POUNDS AS AZLAN ISSUE COLLAPSES

The merchant bank, SBC Warburg, was left with losses of 1 million pounds stg yesterday after the rights issue for Azlan, the computer networking company, collapsed. The bank had to buy 2.22 million shares at 640p each and then sold 1.42 million shares in a pool at 550p. Azlan hoped to buy Akam, a Dutch computing company and was offering its new shares on a three-for-ten basis at 620p each, while its own shares were trading at 740p, but its shares kept falling after they adjusted for the issue, dropping to 566p. The plunge followed the Azlan's flagging growth rate, which was highlighted by the rights issue according to analysts.
THE GUARDIAN

-- UNIONS TRADE PAY FOR JOBS Cement company Blue Circle and two of Britain's largest unions, the GMB general union and the TGWU Transport Union, yesterday reached agreement on a deal offering five years of job security in return for pay restraint and flexible working practices. The European-style deal was hailed by Labour as a model for future employer-employee relations.
-- GIORDANO TAKES PAY CUT

British Gas yesterday bowed to pressure for change at the top with the announcement that chairman Dick Giordano will accept a 50 per cent pay cut. It also emerged that respected former Unilever boss Sir Michael Perry will head household gas business Centrica, soon to be spun off.
-- OLD NUCLEAR REACTORS WIN A REPRIEVE

The Nuclear Installations Inspectorate has approved British Energy's two oldest nuclear power stations for another 10 years of use. The company is hoping to keep as many of its stations in operation as possible in order to preserve its balance sheet so soon after last summer's flotation. The two gas-cooled reactors first started up in 1976.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SPENDING SPREE RAISES RATE FEARS

New figures published by the Bank of England show that the amount of cash in circulation rose above expectations last month, pointing to a strong upward trend in spending. The evidence on the scale of the seasonal spending spree will put the chancellor of the exchequer, Kenneth Clarke under more pressure to raise the cost of borrowing, with the Governor of the Bank of England, Eddie George, likely to urge him to act at next week's monthly meeting.
-- OFWAT SAVAGES SEVERN TRENT

Ofwat, the water industry regulator launched a public assault yesterday on Severn Trent, one of the largest privatized water companies, for failing to meet its investment targets by 100 million pounds stg in just two years. The criticism of Severn Trent coincides with the start of the regulator's comprehensive review of the companies' five-year price limits.
-- AIRBUS PRODUCTION TO DOUBLE AS IT MEETS ORDERS FOR 326 PLANES

European aircraft manufacturer, Airbus Industrie, plans to nearly double production over the coming two years. The plans announced yesterday follow a bumper year for orders in 1996. The announcement is a boost for British Aerospace, which owns a 20 percent stake in Airbus and makes wings for the Airbus range at its Chester plant in North Wales.
